title: Scaling a Spring Boot Monolith: Containers, EC2 Auto Scaling, and Zero-Downtime Deployments
subtitle: How I containerised a single-instance Spring Boot app and built a production-grade auto-scaling architecture on AWS with Aurora multi-region failover and a Jenkins canary pipeline.
overview: The client had a Java Spring Boot monolith running on a single EC2 instance. Traffic was growing and the single-instance model was a single point of failure — one bad deploy or one traffic spike and the service was down. The goal: make it horizontally scalable, resilient to instance failure, and deployable without downtime. Fargate was considered but ruled out — it was relatively new at the time and the client's team was not comfortable operating it in production. The chosen path was EC2-backed ECS clusters with an Auto Scaling Group, giving the team full visibility into the underlying compute while still benefiting from container orchestration.
problem: A single EC2 instance running a Spring Boot JAR cannot absorb traffic spikes — it fails with a hard ceiling. It is also a deployment liability: any deploy takes the service offline. The database was a single RDS instance with no failover, and there was no CI/CD pipeline — developers were SCP-ing JARs to the server. The client needed elasticity, resilience, and a repeatable automated deployment process that did not require a maintenance window.
architecture:
Before:
  Client → EC2 (Spring Boot JAR, stateful JVM heap) → RDS (single instance)
  Deploy: SSH + copy JAR + restart

After:
  Client
    └─ ALB (Application Load Balancer)
         ├─ EC2 Instance 1 (Docker: Spring Boot, stateless)
         ├─ EC2 Instance 2 (Docker: Spring Boot, stateless)
         └─ EC2 Instance N (Auto Scaling Group)
              ↕ CloudWatch Alarms (CPU > 90%, Memory > 85%)
              ↕ Auto Scaling Policy (scale-out + scale-in)

  ElastiCache Redis (Multi-AZ)
    ├─ Session store (Spring Session)
    └─ Application cache (@Cacheable, TTL-based)

  Aurora Global Cluster
    ├─ Primary (Singapore) ← writes
    └─ Read Replica (Hong Kong) ← reads + promoted on failover

  Jenkins Pipeline
    Build → Docker Build → Push ECR → ECS Rolling Deploy → Canary Gate (5%)

implementation.title: Step 1 — Containerise the Spring Boot application
implementation.description: The first step was packaging the Spring Boot application as a Docker image. A multi-stage Dockerfile keeps the final image small: a Maven build stage compiles and packages the JAR, and a slim JRE stage runs it. The image is tagged with the Git commit SHA so every deployment is traceable back to a specific commit.
implementation.code:
# Dockerfile (multi-stage)
FROM maven:3.8-openjdk-17 AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline -q          # cache deps layer
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests -q

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/target/*.jar app.jar

# JVM tuning for containers (respect cgroup memory limits)
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseContainerSupport \
               -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
               -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
               -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom"

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]

# Build and push to ECR
docker build -t my-app:${GIT_SHA} .
docker tag my-app:${GIT_SHA} 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:${GIT_SHA}
docker push 123456789.dkr.ecr.ap-southeast-1.amazonaws.com/my-app:${GIT_SHA}

implementation.title: Step 2 — Externalising state to ElastiCache Redis (prerequisite for scaling)
implementation.description: Before any instance could be added, the application had to become stateless. The original code stored user session data, authentication tokens, and some in-memory caches directly in the JVM heap — which meant two users hitting two different instances would see inconsistent state. The fix: provision an ElastiCache Redis cluster and migrate every piece of shared state out of the application process. Spring Session makes this transparent — switching the session store to Redis requires only a dependency and a config change, no session logic changes in the controllers. In-memory caches (e.g. frequently queried lookup data) were migrated to Redis with TTL-based expiry so any instance can hydrate its local state on demand.

implementation.title: Step 3 — EC2 cluster with Auto Scaling Group (why not Fargate)
implementation.description: Fargate was evaluated but ruled out in 2020 — the client's ops team wanted to be able to SSH into instances, inspect logs directly, and had existing runbooks built around EC2. An ECS cluster backed by an Auto Scaling Group of EC2 instances gave container orchestration without removing the familiar compute layer. ECS places containers onto available instances; the ASG handles adding and removing the underlying VMs.

implementation.title: Step 3 — CloudWatch alarms for CPU and memory triggers
implementation.description: Two CloudWatch alarms gate the scale-out event. CPU is a native EC2 metric. Memory is not — the Amazon CloudWatch Agent must be installed on EC2 instances and configured to push the `mem_used_percent` custom metric. The alarm requires the threshold to be sustained for 5 consecutive 1-minute periods (5 minutes total) before firing, filtering out transient spikes that self-resolve.
implementation.code:
# Scale-Out alarm — CPU
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "my-app-cpu-high" \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 60 \
  --evaluation-periods 5 \
  --threshold 90 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold \
  --dimensions Name=AutoScalingGroupName,Value=my-app-asg \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:autoscaling:ap-southeast-1:123:scalingPolicy/scale-out-policy

# Scale-Out alarm — Memory (custom metric via CloudWatch Agent)
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "my-app-memory-high" \
  --metric-name mem_used_percent \
  --namespace CWAgent \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 60 \
  --evaluation-periods 5 \
  --threshold 85 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanOrEqualToThreshold \
  --dimensions Name=AutoScalingGroupName,Value=my-app-asg \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:autoscaling:ap-southeast-1:123:scalingPolicy/scale-out-policy

# CloudWatch Agent config snippet (on each EC2)
# /opt/aws/amazon-cloudwatch-agent/etc/amazon-cloudwatch-agent.json
{
  "metrics": {
    "namespace": "CWAgent",
    "metrics_collected": {
      "mem": { "measurement": ["mem_used_percent"], "metrics_collection_interval": 60 }
    }
  }
}

implementation.title: Step 4 — Auto Scaling policies: scale-out and scale-in
implementation.description: Scaling operates in two phases. When the CPU alarm fires, the ASG first adds a new EC2 instance (ASG scale-out policy). Once the new instance registers as healthy in the ASG, ECS scheduler detects additional capacity and places a new container task. Scale-in is more cautious — a separate alarm watches for sustained low CPU (<30% for 15 minutes) before terminating an instance. A cooldown period of 300 seconds prevents thrashing.
implementation.code:
# ASG Step Scaling Policy — Scale Out
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy \
  --auto-scaling-group-name my-app-asg \
  --policy-name scale-out \
  --policy-type StepScaling \
  --adjustment-type ChangeInCapacity \
  --step-adjustments \
      MetricIntervalLowerBound=0,MetricIntervalUpperBound=20,ScalingAdjustment=1 \
      MetricIntervalLowerBound=20,ScalingAdjustment=2

# The two-step mechanism:
# Alarm fires
#   └─ ASG adds EC2 instance(s)  ← ASG policy
#        └─ ECS detects new capacity
#             └─ ECS scheduler places container task(s) on new instance

# Scale-in alarm (sustained low CPU for 15 min)
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "my-app-cpu-low" \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 60 \
  --evaluation-periods 15 \
  --threshold 30 \
  --comparison-operator LessThanOrEqualToThreshold \
  --alarm-actions arn:aws:autoscaling:ap-southeast-1:123:scalingPolicy/scale-in-policy

# Scale-in is aggressive with instance protection:
# ECS drains tasks from the instance before the ASG terminates it
# → no in-flight requests are dropped

implementation.title: Step 5 — Application Load Balancer and target groups
implementation.description: The ALB sits in front of the ECS service. It forwards HTTPS traffic on port 443 to ECS tasks on port 8080, terminating TLS at the ALB using an ACM certificate. Health check on `/actuator/health` (Spring Boot Actuator) ensures traffic only reaches fully started tasks. Sticky sessions were disabled — the Spring Boot app was made stateless by externalising session state to ElastiCache Redis.
implementation.code:
# ALB listener rule (HTTPS → ECS target group)
aws elbv2 create-listener \
  --load-balancer-arn arn:aws:elasticloadbalancing:...:loadbalancer/app/my-app-alb \
  --protocol HTTPS \
  --port 443 \
  --certificates CertificateArn=arn:aws:acm:...:certificate/abc123 \
  --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=arn:...targetgroup/my-app-tg

# Target group health check
aws elbv2 modify-target-group \
  --target-group-arn arn:...targetgroup/my-app-tg \
  --health-check-path /actuator/health \
  --health-check-interval-seconds 30 \
  --healthy-threshold-count 2 \
  --unhealthy-threshold-count 3

# Spring Boot: make session stateless (externalise to Redis)
# application-prod.yml
spring:
  session:
    store-type: redis
  redis:
    host: ${REDIS_HOST}
    port: 6379
  security:
    require-ssl: true

implementation.title: Step 6 — Aurora Global Cluster: Singapore primary, Hong Kong failover
implementation.description: A single-region Aurora instance was replaced with an Aurora Global Database spanning Singapore (ap-southeast-1) as the primary writer and Hong Kong (ap-east-1) as a read replica region. In normal operation the app writes to Singapore. The Hong Kong node absorbs read traffic from any HK-based services. In a regional failure, the HK instance can be promoted to primary within minutes — Aurora Global replication lag is typically under 1 second.
implementation.code:
# Aurora Global Cluster setup
aws rds create-global-cluster \
  --global-cluster-identifier my-app-global \
  --engine aurora-mysql \
  --engine-version 8.0.mysql_aurora.3.02.0

# Primary cluster in Singapore
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier my-app-primary \
  --global-cluster-identifier my-app-global \
  --engine aurora-mysql \
  --master-username admin \
  --master-user-password ${DB_PASSWORD} \
  --db-subnet-group-name my-subnet-group-sg \
  --region ap-southeast-1

# Secondary cluster in Hong Kong (replicates from SG)
aws rds create-db-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier my-app-secondary \
  --global-cluster-identifier my-app-global \
  --engine aurora-mysql \
  --db-subnet-group-name my-subnet-group-hk \
  --region ap-east-1

# Failover: promote HK to primary (removes it from global cluster first)
aws rds remove-from-global-cluster \
  --db-cluster-identifier my-app-secondary \
  --global-cluster-identifier my-app-global
# HK cluster becomes standalone primary, <1 min promotion

# Spring Boot datasource routing
# application-prod.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://my-app-primary.cluster-xyz.ap-southeast-1.rds.amazonaws.com:3306/mydb
    # On failover, Route 53 CNAME update points to HK cluster endpoint

implementation.title: Step 7 — Jenkins CI/CD pipeline: build, push, deploy
implementation.description: A Jenkins declarative pipeline replaced the manual SSH-and-copy process. The pipeline builds the Docker image, pushes it to ECR, and triggers an ECS service update. Jenkins credentials store holds the AWS access keys and Docker registry credentials — no secrets in the Jenkinsfile. The pipeline runs on every merge to `main`.

implementation.title: Step 8 — Canary deployment: 5% traffic gate before full cutover
implementation.description: ECS rolling deployment was configured with a canary gate: the new task set receives only 5% of ALB traffic initially. After a 10-minute bake period, automated health checks (error rate, p99 latency via CloudWatch) confirm the new version is healthy. Only then does the ALB shift 100% of traffic to the new tasks and drain the old ones. This means a bad deploy affects at most 5% of users before it is caught and rolled back.
implementation.code:
# ECS deployment circuit breaker + rollback (built-in)
aws ecs update-service \
  --cluster my-app-cluster \
  --service my-app-service \
  --deployment-configuration '{
    "deploymentCircuitBreaker": {
      "enable": true,
      "rollback": true
    },
    "maximumPercent": 200,
    "minimumHealthyPercent": 100
  }'

# Canary traffic split via two ALB target groups
# Target Group A: existing tasks (95%)
# Target Group B: new tasks (5%)
aws elbv2 modify-listener \
  --listener-arn arn:...listener/abc \
  --default-actions Type=forward,ForwardConfig='{
    "TargetGroups": [
      {"TargetGroupArn": "arn:...tg/my-app-stable", "Weight": 95},
      {"TargetGroupArn": "arn:...tg/my-app-canary", "Weight": 5}
    ]
  }'

# After bake period validation (check CloudWatch metrics)
ERROR_RATE=$(aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics \
  --metric-name 5XXError --namespace AWS/ApplicationELB \
  --start-time $(date -u -v-10M +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S) \
  --end-time $(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S) \
  --period 600 --statistics Sum ...)

# If error rate < threshold → shift 100% to new tasks
# Else → rollback: shift 100% back to stable target group

impact: Eliminated the single point of failure — service now survives instance-level failures transparently via ALB health checks and ECS task replacement
Auto Scaling absorbs traffic spikes within 5 minutes of sustained CPU pressure without manual intervention
Aurora Global cross-region replication (SG → HK) provides sub-second replication lag and regional failover capability without manual backup restores
Canary deployment gate reduced production incident risk — a bad deploy affects at most 5% of live traffic before automated rollback fires
Jenkins pipeline replaced manual SSH deploys — reproducible, auditable, and zero-downtime from day one of adoption
lessons: Fargate immaturity was a valid concern in 2020 — team comfort and operational visibility outweigh theoretical simplicity when you are the one carrying the pager at 2am
Memory is not a native EC2 CloudWatch metric — the CloudWatch Agent must be installed on every instance in the ASG launch template, not just manually on existing instances
Scale-in is more dangerous than scale-out — ECS connection draining must be configured correctly or in-flight requests will be dropped when the ASG terminates an instance
A stateless application is a prerequisite for horizontal scaling — externalising session state to Redis was the first code change, before any infrastructure work began
The 5% canary gate is only as useful as the metrics you check during the bake period — define your error rate and latency thresholds before the first deploy, not after the first incident
